1.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Coordinator, Subagents and Spawning
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Coordinator, Subagents and Spawning. This module covers task statements one point two and one point three: coordinators, subagents and spawning. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. The hub-and-spoke (coordinator and subagents) architecture and why all communication goes through the coordinator. Why subagents have isolated context and what that means for prompts. How the coordinator decomposes, delegates, aggregates and refines, and the risk of too narrow a decomposition. How to spawn subagents: the Task tool, allowed Tools, Agent Definition, parallel spawning, forks.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply Researches a Market
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply Researches a Market. Birchwood's analysts ask: "What is changing in home energy?". A coordinator agent splits the question and hands parts to four subagents: web search, document analysis, synthesis and report generation. The final report must be complete and cited.

1.title: The Coordinator and Subagents
1.text: The Coordinator and Subagents. In the hub-and-spoke pattern, one coordinator agent is the hub; the subagents are spokes.

1.title: The Coordinator and Subagents, continued
1.text: The Coordinator and Subagents, continued. The figure shows this: Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator decomposes the task, delegates to subagents, collects results, handles errors and decides what to run next; subagents never talk to each other directly.

1.title: The Coordinator and Subagents, continued
1.text: The Coordinator and Subagents, continued. Decomposes the task and decides which subagents to invoke from the query's complexity. Simple questions should not run the full pipeline. Delegates with clear goals and passes the needed context. Subagents do not share memory. Aggregates results and evaluates them for gaps. Quality control sits in one place. Manages all communication, error handling and information routing. Gives observability, consistent error handling and controlled information flow. Subagents operate with isolated context: they do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history. Route every subagent exchange through the coordinator, not subagent to subagent. Exam tip: "Why route communication through the coordinator?" to observability, consistent error handling, controlled information flow.

1.title: Decomposition: Coverage and Dynamic Selection
1.text: Decomposition: Coverage and Dynamic Selection. Too narrow a decomposition is the classic failure. If the coordinator turns "home energy" into "rooftop solar", "solar inverters" and "solar financing", every subagent can do a perfect job and the report still misses batteries, heat pumps and wind. The root cause is the coordinator's task decomposition, not the downstream agents. Design the coordinator to analyze the query's requirements and choose which subagents to invoke, instead of always running the whole pipeline. Partition the scope to minimize duplication: give each agent a distinct subtopic or source type (for example "market data" versus "academic papers").

1.title: Decomposition: Coverage and Dynamic Selection, continued
1.text: Decomposition: Coverage and Dynamic Selection, continued. Use an iterative refinement loop: the coordinator checks the synthesis for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries to search and analysis agents, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient.

1.title: Decomposition: Coverage and Dynamic Selection, continued
1.text: Decomposition: Coverage and Dynamic Selection, continued. The figure shows this: Iterative refinement: after synthesis the coordinator evaluates coverage, re-delegates targeted queries for gaps, and repeats until coverage is sufficient. Exam tip: When the final output has a missing area but each subagent "succeeded", look at how the coordinator split the task.

1.title: Spawning Subagents
1.text: Spawning Subagents. Spawning tool. Subagents are started by the Task tool. For a coordinator to start them, allowed Tools must include "Task". Agent Definition. Each subagent type has a description (when to use it), a system prompt and tool restrictions. Context. A subagent does not inherit the parent's context or share memory between invocations: put everything it needs in its prompt. Forks. Fork-based session management creates branches to explore divergent approaches from a shared baseline (see Module four).

1.title: Spawning Subagents, continued
1.text: Spawning Subagents, continued. or In current Claude Code and Agent S D K (software development kit) documentation the spawning tool is named Agent; it was renamed from Task in Claude Code version two point one point sixty-three, and Task still works as an alias. The exam guide uses Task and allowed Tools containing "Task". Answer with the guide's wording; in real code include both names or the current one. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six.

1.title: Spawning Subagents, continued
1.text: Spawning Subagents, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Passing context
1.text: Passing context. Include complete findings from earlier agents directly in the next subagent's prompt (for example, the search results and the document analysis go into the synthesis prompt). Use a structured format that separates content from metadata (claim, source U R L (uniform resource locator), document name, page number, date) so attribution survives the hand-off. Spawn in parallel by emitting several Task tool calls in one coordinator response, not across separate turns; parallel calls cut latency. Write coordinator prompts that give the goal and the quality criteria, not a step-by-step procedure, so subagents can adapt.

1.title: Passing context, continued
1.text: Passing context, continued. The figure shows this: Subagents start fresh: they see their own system prompt and the prompt the coordinator writes, not the coordinator's history or other subagents' results. Current documentation: a subagent's final message returns to the parent as a summary, so verbose intermediate work stays out of the parent's context; subagents can run in parallel and (by default) can themselves spawn subagents up to three levels below the main agent. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: A subagent that "does not know" something almost always means the coordinator never put it in the prompt: subagents do not inherit context or memory.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Pattern: Hub-and-spoke: coordinator plus subagents; all communication via the coordinator. Why via coordinator: Observability, consistent error handling, controlled information flow. Subagent context: Isolated; does not inherit history or share memory; give it everything in its prompt. Spawning: Task tool (now called Agent); allowed Tools must include it; Agent Definition equals description plus prompt plus tool limits. Parallel: Several Task calls in one coordinator response. Decomposition risk: Too narrow to incomplete coverage though every subagent "succeeded". Refinement loop: Check gaps to re-delegate targeted queries to re-run synthesis until covered. Prompts: Coordinator gives goals and criteria, not procedures; pass content plus metadata in structured form.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Birchwood's research system produces a report on "the future of home energy" that covers only solar power. Logs show each subagent finished successfully and the coordinator created three subtasks, all about solar panels. What is the most likely root cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The logs show the coordinator assigned only solar subtasks. The subagents did what they were assigned; the gap comes from the decomposition.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which is the main reason to route all subagent communication through the coordinator? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The hub-and-spoke pattern centralizes monitoring, errors and routing in one place.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A coordinator always runs search, analysis, synthesis and reporting for every request, even a one-line factual question. What change is most appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A coordinator should select subagents dynamically based on complexity instead of always running the full pipeline.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. The synthesis subagent produces summaries with missing citations. It receives only the instruction "combine the findings", while the coordinator holds the search results in its own conversation. What is the best fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Subagents do not inherit context; everything required, including attribution metadata, must be in the prompt.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A coordinator must delegate a search and a document analysis that do not depend on each other. How should it start them to minimize latency? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Multiple Task calls in one coordinator response let independent subagents run in parallel.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A coordinator's allowed Tools list contains only Read and Grep, and no subagent ever starts. What is missing? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. To invoke subagents, the coordinator's allowed Tools must include the Task tool (named Agent in current documentation).

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which coordinator prompt follows the recommended style? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Specify goals and quality criteria so subagents can adapt, rather than a rigid procedure.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. After synthesis, the coordinator notices that the report has no data on the Asian market. What should it do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The iterative refinement loop re-delegates for gaps and repeats until coverage is sufficient.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. A research subagent returns summaries without citations. Which two changes help most? The five options are on the screen. The answers are D and E. Subagents do not inherit context, so attribution must be passed in and must be produced as structured output. Peer messaging bypasses the coordinator and dropping citations loses provenance.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Select two. Which two are benefits of routing all subagent communication through the coordinator? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. A central hub gives observability, consistent error handling and controlled information flow. It does not remove the need for prompts or guarantee lower token use.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: C. Question four: B. Question five: C. Question six: D. Question seven: B. Question eight: A. Question nine: D and E. Question ten: A and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
